name: Second Council of Lyon
teaser: Lyon, 1274. Pope Gregory X held a general council at which envoys of the emperor Michael VIII professed the Latin faith and Rome's primacy, and which taught that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as from one source.
knownFor: The council at which the Greek envoys accepted union with Rome. Gennadios Scholarios says a great synod overturned it after Michael VIII's death.
datesNote: 1274. Glassberger says it opened on the feast of the apostles Philip and James, which his Quaracchi editors give as 1 May; Thomas Creyghton, the 1660 editor of Syropoulos, gives 7 May. Glassberger says the Greek envoys came before it ended, and Creyghton says they arrived the next month. Eubel, editor of the Franciscan bullarium, dates Bonaventure's death during the council to 15 July 1274. No held source gives the closing day
issue: Gregory X had sent Jerome of Ascoli and other friars to the Greeks, to bring the Greeks and the Tatars back to the unity of the church (Glassberger). At the opening, Glassberger says, he told of a dream in which Christ promised that the church would win back through him the Holy Land and the Greeks.

The doctrine at stake was how the Holy Spirit proceeds, and the primacy of the Roman church (the council's constitution and Michael VIII's profession). Thomas Aquinas set out for the council carrying the little book he had written against the Greeks at Pope Urban's order (William of Tocco's Life).

Michael VIII's motive, as later writers give it: Gennadios Scholarios says he wanted to ward off the Latins' revenge for the city and make his rule safe for himself and his sons; the chronicle printed under Sphrantzes's name says he sent envoys for union if only to block an expedition by Baldwin and Charles of Anjou; the Latin Directorium of 1332, in Jean Miélot's French, says he feared Charles would take his empire and turned to tricks.

No Greek text from the time against the union is among our sources. Patriarch Joseph I's refusal is held only in later Greek memory (the Synaxaristes; the patriarch list of Nikephoros Kallistos, in PG 147).
calledBy: Pope Gregory X. Glassberger says he began to hold at Lyon the general council he had called, and a witness at the canonization of Thomas Aquinas says Gregory was calling the council when Thomas was summoned to it. The constitution and the conclave decree speak in his name, with the approval of the council. His letter of summons is not among our sources
attended: Manuel Kalekas, a Greek Dominican who wrote for the Latins and died in 1410, gives the pope in person and about 400 bishops, with envoys standing in for the church of Constantinople (Adversus Graecos, in Ambrogio Traversari's Latin). His editor Fabricius says Kalekas did not live at the time of the council. No list of names is among our sources.

The Greek envoys go unnamed in Glassberger and in Gennadios. Thomas Creyghton, the 1660 editor, names them as Theophanes, metropolitan of Nicaea, and Germanos, who had been patriarch some years before, between Arsenios and Joseph. Guillaume Adam, a Latin hostile to the Greeks writing about 1317, says the emperor sent his patriarch; the editors of the Recueil identify that patriarch as John Bekkos (see uncertain).
Their interpreter was John of Balastri (Parastron), a Franciscan of Constantinople who knew Greek and Latin, interpreter at Lyon for the emperor and the Greek prelates (Glassberger).

Glassberger says three Franciscan prelates presided by the pope's order and handled the council's business: Cardinal Bonaventure, Eudes Rigaud, archbishop of Rouen, and the bishop of Tripoli, whom Eubel names as Paul.
Envoys of the Tatars came in robes woven with gold to make an alliance, and one of them, a king's son, was baptized, with the pope lifting him from the font (Glassberger).
Thomas Aquinas was summoned and was on the road in Lent, by a witness at his canonization, when he fell ill at Maenza (Tocco's Life; the deposition of Nicholas, abbot of Fossanova).
decided: A constitution on the procession of the Holy Spirit. It confesses that the Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son, as from one principle and by one spiration, and, with the approval of the council, condemns those who deny it or say he proceeds from them as from two principles (the acts, in Denzinger).

The profession of faith of Michael VIII, offered to Gregory X at the council. It confesses the Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, purgatory, seven sacraments, that the Roman church makes the eucharist from unleavened bread, and the supreme and full primacy of the Roman church over the whole Catholic church, whose judgment settles questions of faith (the text, in Denzinger). Bannwart, Denzinger's editor, notes that Clement IV had put it to Michael in 1267.

The conclave decree Ubi periculum. When a pope dies, the cardinals wait ten days for the absent ones, then live together in one room in the palace, closed so that no one can go in or out. If they have not chosen within three days, they get one dish at lunch and supper for the next five; after that, only bread, wine and water, until a pope is chosen (the acts, in Mirbt).

On the mendicant orders, the text of the decree is not among our sources. Salimbene, a Franciscan of the time, says in Coulton's English that Gregory forbade new orders such as the Sack friars and the Apostles. Glassberger says only the Friars Minor and the Preachers were kept, the others dissolved until something else was ordered. Clement XIV in 1773 says Gregory banned for ever the mendicant orders founded after the Fourth Lateran Council without the apostolic see's confirmation, and Lea says the Carmelites and Augustinians were left on sufferance (see uncertain).
Glassberger says the pope charged the bishops, and above all the Franciscans and Dominicans, to preach the cross in aid of the Holy Land.
outcome: Glassberger says the Greeks recognized the primacy of the Roman church and afterwards fell back into their old errors.

The chronicle printed under Sphrantzes's name says the union rested on three heads: the pope named in the hymns, appeal to him, and his first place in all things. The clergy would not keep quiet and stirred up the crowd; the emperor said it was done by oikonomia, as a concession, and flogged, ill-treated and exiled many who would not be persuaded.
Gennadios Scholarios says the emperor had told the church the union was a concession, but chose envoys who knew his mind, and they came back bringing open Latinism.

Patriarch Joseph I would not accept the union and gave up his throne, the Synaxaristes says; the patriarch list in PG 147 says Michael drove him out for it. John Bekkos took his place and made the union with the Latins (the patriarch list; the Synaxaristes).

The Synaxaristes remembers the twenty-six monks of Zographou and Euthymios, abbot of Vatopedi, with twelve of his monks, as martyrs who rebuked the Latin-minded Michael and Bekkos. Philipp Meyer, the modern editor of the Athos charters, doubts the story of a punitive invasion of Athos.
The editors of the Recueil say Michael signed the act of union in 1277 and that Martin IV excommunicated him on 18 November 1281.

After Michael's death, Gennadios says, a great synod overturned the act of Lyon. The patriarch list says Andronikos II cast Bekkos down and sent him into exile. Ismaël Boulliau, Doukas's 17th-century editor, says Andronikos denied his father funeral pomp and the usual honors because he had sided with the Latins.

In the Latin church the conclave decree was taken up: a council at Ravenna in 1311 ordered the prayers and processions it set for a vacant Roman see to be held for vacant cathedrals of its province. In 1309 Clement V gave the Oxford Franciscans the Sack friars' house, which was expected soon to fall to the apostolic see under Gregory's constitution, and Boniface VIII later set the Augustinian Hermits and the Carmelites on a firm footing, as before the council (Glassberger).

In 1870 the First Vatican Council recalled that, with the approval of the Second Council of Lyon, the Greeks professed the supreme and full primacy of the Roman church (Pastor aeternus, in Mirbt and in Schaff's English).

record.witness: Constitution on the procession of the Holy Spirit (Denzinger, ed. Bannwart)
record.note: The council's own text, in a modern editor's extract from Mansi; speaks for Gregory X with the council's approval.

record.witness: Profession of faith of Michael VIII (Denzinger, ed. Bannwart)
record.note: Offered at the council in the emperor's name; Bannwart says Clement IV first put it to him in 1267.

record.witness: Salimbene of Parma, Chronicle (in G. G. Coulton's English, From St. Francis to Dante)
record.note: A Franciscan of the time; in Coulton's selected English, with his Latin on the mendicant ruling quoted by Glassberger's editors.
A Franciscan chronicler writing in 1508, citing earlier Franciscan chronicles; pro-council, and the main narrative of the scene.

record.witness: William of Tocco's Life of Thomas Aquinas and the depositions at his canonization (Acta Sanctorum)
record.note: Dominican; one deponent is the abbot of Fossanova, where Thomas lay ill.

record.witness: Manuel Kalekas, Adversus Graecos (PG 152, in Traversari's Latin)
record.note: Greek on the Latin side; died 1410; the only witness for about 400 bishops.

record.witness: Gennadios Scholarios, on the addition to the Creed (PG 160)
The chronicle printed under Sphrantzes's name (Bonn 1838)
record.note: Greek, critical of Michael; names the wrong pope and does not name Lyon.

record.witness: Nikephoros Kallistos's list of the patriarchs (PG 147)
record.note: Greek, against the union; written about 1300, under Andronikos II; Migne's Latin mistranslates Joseph's line, so the Greek is followed.
Orthodox liturgical memory of those who refused.

record.witness: Guillaume Adam (about 1317) and the Directorium of 1332, in the Recueil des historiens des croisades
record.note: Latin writers hostile to the Greeks and to Michael.

record.witness: Joseph of Methone's dialogue on Florence (PG 159)
record.note: A Greek unionist who puts in an opponent's mouth the claim that Lyon condemned the Latins.

record.witness: Thomas Creyghton, Boulliau, Eubel, Bannwart, Mirbt, the Recueil editors, Philipp Meyer and H. C. Lea
record.note: Editors and historians who give the envoys' names, dates, the excommunication of 1281 and the details of the mendicant ruling.

traditions.name: The Latin Papal Church (Gregorian Reform to Innocent III)
traditions.note: Gregory X called and led the council, and its constitution and conclave decree speak in his name with the council's approval.

traditions.name: The Franciscan Movement
traditions.note: Bonaventure, Eudes Rigaud and the bishop of Tripoli presided by the pope's order, by Glassberger's Franciscan account; the interpreter for the Greeks was a friar.

traditions.name: The Dominican Order
traditions.note: Thomas Aquinas was summoned with his book against the Greeks and fell ill on the way (Tocco's Life); the pope charged the Preachers, with the Minors, to preach the cross (Glassberger).

traditions.name: The Byzantine Church after the Schism
traditions.note: Its envoys professed the faith and the primacy at Lyon; Patriarch Joseph would not accept the union, and after Michael's death a great synod overturned it (the Synaxaristes; Nikephoros Kallistos's patriarch list; Gennadios).

traditions.name: Athonite & Comnenian Byzantine Monasticism
traditions.note: The Synaxaristes remembers the monks of Zographou and Vatopedi as martyrs who rebuked Michael and Bekkos; Philipp Meyer doubts the story of an invasion of Athos.

traditions.name: The Carmelites
traditions.note: Left to exist on sufferance until further order, by H. C. Lea's account, where Glassberger has all orders but the Minors and Preachers dissolved; later set on a firm footing by Boniface VIII, as before the council (Glassberger).

traditions.name: Military-Religious Orders (Templars, Hospitallers)
traditions.note: Gregory X tried in vain at the council to unite the orders, by H. C. Lea's modern account only.

people.name: Gregory X
people.part: Called and led the council; received the Greek envoys with a kiss and celebrated the Mass at which they sang the Creed (Glassberger)

people.name: Bonaventure
people.part: Cardinal; presided, by the Franciscan account; preached on the Greeks' coming; died while the council sat

people.name: Thomas Aquinas
people.part: Summoned; set out with his book against the Greeks and fell ill on the road

people.name: Michael VIII Palaiologos
people.part: Emperor; not present; sent envoys and the profession of faith offered in his name

people.name: Jerome of Ascoli
people.part: Legate to the Greeks; brought their envoys to Lyon; elected Franciscan minister general there while away

people.name: Eudes Rigaud
people.part: Archbishop of Rouen; presided, by the Franciscan account

people.name: Paul of Tripoli
people.part: Bishop; presided, by the Franciscan account (named by Eubel)

people.name: John of Balastri (Parastron)
people.part: Franciscan of Constantinople; interpreter for the emperor and the Greek prelates

people.name: Germanos
people.part: Former patriarch; envoy, by Creyghton's modern account only

people.name: Theophanes of Nicaea
people.part: Metropolitan; envoy, by Creyghton's modern account only

people.name: Joseph I of Constantinople
people.part: Patriarch; not present; refused the union and lost his throne

people.name: John Bekkos
people.part: Not shown at Lyon by any held line of the time; patriarch after Joseph, he carried the union; exiled under Andronikos II

people.name: Euthymios of Vatopedi
people.part: Not present; rebuked Michael and Bekkos, by the Synaxaristes

people.name: Andronikos II Palaiologos
people.part: Not present; cast Bekkos down after Michael's death

people.name: Clement IV
people.part: Dead; had put the profession to Michael in 1267, by Bannwart's note

people.name: Martin IV
people.part: Not present; excommunicated Michael in 1281, by the Recueil editors

uncertain: Of the council's acts, only three texts are among our sources, in modern editors' extracts: the constitution on the Spirit, Michael VIII's profession and the conclave decree. The scene comes from Glassberger, a Franciscan writing in 1508. No Greek account from the time is among our sources; the Greek side, both for and against the union, reaches us from later writers, the earliest the patriarch list of Nikephoros Kallistos from about 1300.
The opening day: 1 May by Glassberger's feast day, as his editors give it; 7 May in Creyghton, the 1660 editor of Syropoulos.
The count of about 400 bishops rests on Kalekas alone, a late writer giving a round number.
That the three Franciscans presided rests on Franciscan writers alone, Glassberger and Eubel.

What the mendicant decree did: Glassberger says all orders but the Minors and Preachers were dissolved; Clement XIV and Lea say it struck only unconfirmed orders, and Lea that the Carmelites and Augustinians were left on sufferance.

Who the Greek envoys were: Creyghton names Theophanes of Nicaea and the former patriarch Germanos; Guillaume Adam, hostile, says the emperor sent his patriarch, whom the Recueil editors call Bekkos, though their own note makes Bekkos a resister in 1274 who was won over later.
How Joseph lost his throne: the Synaxaristes says he gave it up; the patriarch list in PG 147 says Michael drove him out.

Michael's motive: Gennadios, the Sphrantzes chronicle and the Directorium say he wished to ward off the Latins' revenge or Charles of Anjou's attack. The Recueil editors, modern, say the Greeks hoped to win the Western princes' favor and support.
The Athonite martyrs are held in liturgical memory; Meyer thinks the story of an invasion may be confused with a Catalan raid after 1300.

What Lyon decided, in later Greek memory: Gennadios remembers it as a union on Latin terms, and Doukas sets it beside Florence as a union sworn under oaths; a unionist dialogue has an opponent claim it condemned the Latins and that the acts were corrupted.
How Michael was buried: Boulliau says without funeral pomp and the usual honors; Creyghton and Guillaume Adam say he was left unburied.
